title: Procurement Management
sequence: Planning (sourcing strategy, make-or-buy, procurement plan, documents); conducting procurement (solicit, select, negotiate, award) and administering contracts run through Executing and Monitoring & Controlling; contract closure belongs to Closing (Topic 35).

Planning (sourcing strategy, make-or-buy, procurement plan, documents); conducting procurement (solicit, select, negotiate, award) and administering contracts run through Executing and Monitoring & Controlling; contract closure belongs to Closing (Topic 35).

PMBOK 8 does not treat procurement as a separate performance domain, because project procurement usually runs through the organization's procurement department, policies and vendor relationships. The older PMBOK 6 process names (Plan, Conduct, Control and Close Procurements) used in the course slides are replaced by Plan Sourcing Strategy plus the practices in Appendix X4. The ECO tasks above still apply.
[Beyond PMBOK 8] = exam-relevant, but PMBOK 8 does not spell it out (ECO wording, common exam practice, mock-exam style).

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Procurement Acquiring goods, services or results from external sources to meet project objectives
Buyer / seller Buyer: the entity that purchases. Seller (vendor, contractor, supplier): the entity that provides. Their relationship involves information asymmetry and is a source of risk
Agreement Any document or communication that defines initial intentions: contract, purchase order, service-level agreement (SLA), memorandum of understanding or agreement (MOU/MOA), letter of agreement. May be simple or complex; a project can have several in parallel or in sequence; must comply with local, national and international law
Statement of work (SOW) Describes the work or deliverables to be purchased
Sourcing strategy plan Which elements are insourced, outsourced or both, with the rationale (value, schedule, risk, finance), plus source selection criteria
Procurement management plan How the team acquires goods and services from outside the organization (section 3.3)
Procurement documentation All documents used to sign, execute and close an agreement: SOW, payment information, contractor performance information, plans, drawings, correspondence
Make-or-buy Deciding whether work is best done by the project team or bought
Bid documents RFI (request for information), RFP (request for proposal), RFQ (request for quote), IFB / ITT (invitation for bid or to tender)
Letter of intent Beyond PMBOK 8 A non-binding statement that the buyer intends to contract with a seller; it is not a contract
Source selection Choosing the seller using predefined, weighted criteria
Claim Beyond PMBOK 8definition A request or assertion by a party for payment, time or other relief under the agreement, often arising from changes or variation orders (PMBOK 8 names variation orders as a leading source of disputable claims)
ADR Alternative dispute resolution: negotiation, mediation, arbitration, dispute review boards, expert determination (litigation is the last resort)
Liquidated damages Beyond PMBOK 8 Pre-agreed compensation payable by a party for a specified breach, such as late delivery
Performance bond / insurance Instruments the procurement plan may require to mitigate risk (Topic 21)

2Procurement Overview and Flow

Three stages (PMBOK 8 Appendix X4):

  1. Plan: identify needs; involve key stakeholders early; analyze needs and decide whether to buy; set procurement standards, rules and regulations; identify potential sellers; prepare procurement documents.
  2. Conduct: obtain responses, evaluate, select, negotiate and award. The process must be transparent and fair, with equal opportunity for all potential sellers and bidder questions (RFIs) answered adequately and to everyone. Choose on predefined criteria such as cost, quality and the ability to meet requirements and timelines.
  3. Monitor, control and close: manage relationships, monitor contract performance, make changes and corrections, and close the contracts, confirming all obligations were met and nothing is outstanding.

Who does what: the people authorized to procure may be project team members, management or the purchasing department. Negotiation is led by a procurement team member with authority to sign contracts; the project manager and team assist. Good practice: strong procurement policies, automation, and monitoring with KPIs.

3Plan Procurement and Strategy (ECO)

3.1 Plan Sourcing Strategy (Governance domain)

  • Purpose: document sourcing decisions, specify the source selection approach, define the scope of work for external sourcing and choose appropriate contracts and sources; a clear framework for what to acquire, how and when, internally or externally.
  • Participants: include purchasing or procurement and the buyer's legal department; document responsibilities in the plan.
  • Not the same as Plan Resource Management: resource planning is about acquiring and leading resources; sourcing is about outsourcing work and deliverables (scope, time, cost, quality and resources to acquire from outside) (Topic 19).
  • Tools: expert judgment, market research (industry and seller capabilities from conferences, reviews and other sources), make-or-buy analysis, source selection analysis, document analysis.
  • Output: the sourcing strategy plan (insourcing or outsourcing decisions; source selection criteria).

3.2 Make-or-buy

Advantages of insourcing (make) Advantages of outsourcing (buy)
Uses internal expertise when available Uses external expertise when missing internally
Often cheaper when substantial new innovation is needed Often cheaper when the goods or services are common
Tighter integration with strategic advantage or value proposition Frees capacity and capital to focus on competitive strengths
More control and oversight of deliverables Transfers delivery risk to the supplier; maintains supplier relations

Factors: current resource allocation, skills and abilities, need for specialized or independent expertise, wish to avoid expanding permanent employment obligations, and the risks of each option. The analysis may use payback period, ROI, IRR, discounted cash flow, NPV or cost-benefit analysis (Topic 10).

3.3 The procurement management plan

Element Content
Coordination How procurement links to schedule development and control and other project aspects
Timetable and metrics Key procurement dates; metrics used to manage contracts
Roles and authority Stakeholder roles, and the project team's authority and constraints when a procurement department exists
Constraints and assumptions Anything that could affect planned purchases
Legal and money Legal jurisdiction and payment currency
Bidding approach International, national or local competitive bidding; funding alignment if externally financed
Independent estimates Whether they are used or needed as evaluation criteria
Risk management Performance bonds or insurance to mitigate risks
Prequalified sellers If any

3.4 The procurement strategy

Decide the delivery method, the type of legally binding agreement and how procurement advances through phases.

  • Professional services: buyer and provider with no subcontracting; with subcontracting allowed; joint venture; provider acting as the buyer's representative.
  • Industrial, integration or build-out supply: turnkey, design-build (DB), design-bid-build (DBB), design-build-operate (DBO), build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) and others.
  • Integrated project delivery (IPD): one multiparty agreement (owner, designer, contractor), shared risks and rewards, early involvement, collaborative decisions, open-book accounting.
  • Procurement phases: sequence and objectives, performance indicators and milestones, criteria for moving to the next phase, a monitoring and evaluation plan, and a process for knowledge transfer to later phases.

3.5 Develop a delivery solution (ECO) Beyond PMBOK 8as a named item

Choose how the need will actually be met: build, buy, lease, adapt or partner. Compare options with alternative analysis, multicriteria decision analysis and cost-benefit analysis; favor options that deliver value early and reduce risk. Example: if an off-the-shelf product meets about 80% of the need and a custom build would take a year, buy now and close the gap incrementally. Align the plan with the vendor's way of working.

4Bid Process and Source Selection

Bid documents (PMBOK 8):

Document Use
RFI Gather market information before sending bid documents to selected vendors
RFP Complex or complicated scope where the buyer wants the vendor to propose a solution
RFQ Price is the main factor and the solution is readily available
IFB / ITT Named in PMBOK 8 (X4.2) without detail. Beyond PMBOK 8 Formal call for bids; evaluation mostly on price against a defined specification

Flow: prepare the SOW and high-level estimates; advertise; RFI; qualified sellers; prepare bid documents; bidder conference (answer questions and clarify, the same information to all); proposals or quotes; evaluation and source selection; negotiate terms; contract.

Selection methods (PMBOK 8): least cost; qualifications only; quality-based (highest technical proposal score); quality and cost based; single source; fixed budget (see the diagram for when each applies). Review the priorities of the competing demands before choosing, and publish the evaluation method in the tender documents so bidders know how they will be judged, which builds trust.

Criteria and weights: score each criterion (number, color code or description), weight them by importance, rank proposals by weighted score and use the ranking to set the negotiation sequence. Typical criteria include capability and capacity, product and life cycle cost, delivery dates, technical approach, experience and past performance, key team qualifications, financial stability, compliance expertise, knowledge transfer and training, and sustainability credentials.

Mandatory minimum [Beyond PMBOK 8 — exam practice]: a minimum score on a must-have criterion (for example technical capability) is applied first. A bidder below the minimum is disqualified even with the highest weighted total; the remaining bidders are then ranked by weighted score.

Fair process (ethics, Topic 06): equal information for all bidders; follow the published criteria (including past performance); follow the organization's gift and conflict-of-interest policy; never steer the award to a favored provider.

5Contract Types (ECO: select preferred contract types)

Type What it is Client view Contractor view
Fixed-price Predetermined fee for a clearly defined scope; cost risk on the seller Budget certainty; possible risk premium Profit if efficient; bears overruns
Cost-reimbursable Seller's actual costs plus a fee; used when scope is uncertain or risk is high Flexible; cost escalation risk on the buyer Less financial risk; limited profit
Time and materials (T&M) Actual time and materials plus a margin; hybrid; smaller projects, maintenance, unclear scope Flexible; needs close monitoring Costs covered; scrutiny of time and resources
Target-cost A target cost with sharing of savings and overruns Encourages cost control; needs clear target and rules Incentive to be efficient; bears part of an overrun

Choosing the type (ECO): clear, stable scope → fixed-price (buyer wants certainty). Uncertain scope or high risk (research, complex construction) → cost-reimbursable with cost controls. Scope still evolving but exposure must be capped → T&M with a not-to-exceed value Beyond PMBOK 8wording. Wish to share efficiency gains → target-cost or incentive terms. Evolving requirements in agile work → agile contracting built on incremental deliveries (for example T&M with iteration-based deliverables) so scope can flex.

Emerging practices (PMBOK 8): agile, collaborative (shared risk or reward, caps, reduced rates, performance incentives), outcome-based, sustainable (ESG) and smart (blockchain) contracting; AI tools help analyze contracts, assess risk and predict overruns.

Variants [Beyond PMBOK 8]: firm fixed-price, fixed-price incentive fee, fixed-price with economic price adjustment; cost plus fixed fee, cost plus incentive fee, cost plus award fee.

Think from both sides: a project manager is often both a buyer (contracting vendors) and a seller (contracted by a client). Structure contracts so they benefit all parties (win-win).

6Negotiation (ECO: determine a negotiation strategy; participate in agreement negotiations)

  • Purpose: clarify the structure, rights and obligations and other terms so both parties agree before signing. Final contract language must reflect everything agreed. It ends with a signed contract or other formal agreement.
  • Who: led by a procurement team member with authority to sign contracts; the project manager and team support with technical and project knowledge.
  • Almost everything is negotiable: cost, delivery and payment dates, location of work, intellectual property ownership.

Strategy checklist [Beyond PMBOK 8 structure]:

  1. Clarify your priorities (cost, schedule, quality, risk, relationship), what you can accept, what you can trade, and your alternatives if no deal is reached.
  2. Understand the other side's interests, not only its stated position.
  3. Use facts: independent estimates, market research, past performance.
  4. Look for options that serve both parties, for example payments tied to milestones or validated results (this aligns the vendor with the buyer's goal of learning before committing).
  5. Do not waive rights while preserving the relationship; record agreements in the contract.
  6. Match the approach to the context: a sole source or long-term partner favors collaboration; a commodity purchase favors competition.

7Manage Suppliers and Contracts (ECO: execute the plan; evaluate vendor performance; verify objectives)

Activity What to do
Monitor performance Compare against the contract, SOW and procurement metrics; regular and milestone status updates from contractors; scheduled status reviews and walkthroughs to confirm reports are accurate and complete
Inspect, test and accept Verify deliverables against acceptance criteria and contract performance parameters (Topic 15); a miss is handled under the contract terms (notify formally, require correction, withhold acceptance as the contract allows)
Control changes Contract changes and variation orders go through formal change control and a signed amendment; verbal side deals and free upgrades still need impact assessment (Topic 29)
Pay per terms Payments follow the agreement and acceptance; keep records
Manage the relationship and roles Clarify who directs whose people (for example vendor supervisors and the team) and reporting lines; keep communication open (Topic 20)
Audit A procurement audit is a structured review of contracts and contracting processes for completeness, accuracy and effectiveness; audit rights and obligations belong in the contract; findings go to both project managers
Manage risk Performance bonds, insurance, liquidated damages and dependencies; when a sole-source supplier is late, build a joint recovery plan while preserving contract rights
Evaluate vendor performance Record delivery, quality, cost and responsiveness against agreed measures; keep it in organizational records (lessons learned, vendor performance history) for future selection
Verify that objectives of the agreement are met Confirm deliverables, acceptance, warranties, knowledge transfer and training obligations were delivered; check before closing
Close Resolve open disputes and payments; close all contracts before the project is closed; archive procurement documentation; capture lessons learned (Topic 35)

Source note: PMBOK 8 itself supplies the status updates and walkthroughs for contracted work, the procurement audit, make-or-buy and closing contracts; the rest of the table is standard contract-administration practice that scenario questions use Beyond PMBOK 8.

Vendors as stakeholders: align the project plan with the vendor's way of working (PMBOK 8 Table 2-9 check) and engage vendors as part of the stakeholder strategy (Topic 13).

8Claims and Disputes

  • Disputes rise with project complexity and number of stakeholders; variation orders and time and cost overruns are leading causes. In construction, direct dispute costs have been reported at about 0.5% to 5% of contract value.
  • PMBOK 8 ADR methods: negotiation, mediation, arbitration, dispute review boards, expert determination and litigation (last resort). The ladder in the diagram orders them by formality as a study aid.
  • Project manager's role: understand contract terms; keep detailed records of activities, changes and communications; communicate openly; spot conflict early; build negotiation and conflict skills (you are usually first to engage); work with legal.
  • Care and ethics: be careful with written language (email can become evidence); set escalation protocols; protect confidentiality; stay impartial and factual.

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Scope definition Detailed SOW and specification before bidding Evolving requirements; outcomes and backlog guide the work Detailed SOW for fixed parts; flexible terms for evolving parts
Contract type Fixed-price for well-defined work; cost-reimbursable for uncertain; T&M with ceiling Agile or collaborative contracts: T&M with iteration-based deliverables, caps, incentives, outcome-based pricing Mixed contracts
Delivery and acceptance Milestone-based acceptance Incremental deliveries and acceptance per increment Both
Change control Formal contract change orders Backlog changes inside agreed boundaries; formal approval above contract thresholds Both
Vendor integration Vendor reports to the project manager Vendor staff work in the team; roles and reporting lines clarified Both
Payment Milestones, completion Per iteration or increment; milestone-based smart contracts possible Mixed

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor by size and value (small purchases: qualifications-only or simple agreements), risk, scope clarity, regulatory setting (public procurement rules, international bidding), organizational procurement policies, and market (sole-source situations).
  • Interactions: finance (contract type moves cost risk; payments; funding limits), schedule (lead times, vendor dependencies), resources (external team members and physical resources), risk (transfer, bonds, insurance, supplier and geopolitical risk such as sanctions: assess and plan alternatives early), quality (supplier quality, audits, acceptance), governance (authority and thresholds), stakeholders (vendors, regulators).
  • Check results: plans integrate the supplier's perspective (align your plan with the vendor's way of working); procurement processes, efficiency checks, orders, manufacture and delivery tracking are managed (PMBOK 8 Tables 2-9 and 2-10).

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Make-or-buy first: outsource for missing expertise, a temporary need, or to avoid permanent headcount; compare options with analysis.
  2. Contract type follows scope clarity and risk: defined scope → fixed-price; uncertain scope or high risk → cost-reimbursable; evolving scope with a cap → T&M with not-to-exceed; agile work → agile contracts with incremental delivery.
  3. Fixed-price shifts cost risk to the seller; cost-reimbursable keeps it with the buyer. Know the view of both parties.
  4. Follow the published criteria, including past performance. Price alone is not the rule, and criteria are not changed after bids arrive.
  5. Treat all bidders alike: answer questions for everyone, use the same information, respect gift and conflict policies.
  6. The negotiator with authority to sign leads; the project manager supports with facts. Prepare priorities and alternatives before negotiating.
  7. Align the deal with your goal: for example tie payments to validated results when you need to learn before committing.
  8. A vendor miss is handled under the contract: notify formally, require correction, withhold acceptance as allowed; do not fix it quietly yourself or accept it.
  9. Changes, even free upgrades, go through change control and a signed amendment; no verbal agreements.
  10. Sole-source vendor in trouble: build a joint recovery plan and preserve contract rights rather than just calculating penalties.
  11. Clarify roles and reporting lines between vendor supervisors and your team.
  12. Close all contracts before closing the project: resolve disputes and payments; client acceptance alone is not enough.
  13. Escalate disputes in steps: negotiation first, then ADR; keep records; stay factual and impartial.
  14. Record vendor performance for future decisions (organizational assets).
  15. Follow the sourcing route in the plan (for example the PMO resource pool) and procurement dual-source rules.
  16. Do not use PMBOK 6 process names as the "PMBOK 8 answer"; know the practices, which the ECO still tests.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A hybrid program needs three months of specialized geotechnical testing that no one in the organization can perform, and hiring would add permanent headcount. What should the project manager do?

  • AHire a permanent specialist and keep the person busy after the testing ends
  • BTrain existing staff for a year and delay the testing until they are ready
  • CBuy the service from an external provider after a make-or-buy analysis
  • DPostpone the testing to a later phase when internal capacity may exist
Show the answer

Answer: C. Missing expertise, a temporary need and the wish to avoid permanent obligations favor outsourcing, supported by a make-or-buy analysis. Hiring adds lasting cost, training takes too long and postponing leaves the need unmet.

S2A research-style project has uncertain scope and high risk, and the buyer accepts the cost risk in return for flexibility. Which contract type fits best?

  • AFirm fixed-price, because the buyer wants certainty about the final cost
  • BA lump-sum contract with penalties for any change to the scope
  • CCost-reimbursable, with cost controls to limit escalation
  • DFixed-price with economic price adjustment for inflation over the term
Show the answer

Answer: C. Cost-reimbursable contracts suit uncertain scope or high risk, with the buyer carrying the cost-escalation risk and applying controls. Fixed-price and lump-sum forms put cost risk on a seller who cannot price unknown work.

S3The buyer and a contractor both want an incentive to control cost on a defined building project, sharing savings and overruns. Which contract type fits?

  • ACost-plus fixed fee, in which the buyer pays whatever the work turns out to cost
  • BFirm fixed-price, in which the contractor keeps every saving and bears every overrun
  • CTime and materials without a limit, billed at agreed rates and unit prices
  • DTarget-cost, with an agreed target and a rule for sharing savings and overruns
Show the answer

Answer: D. Target-cost contracts set a target cost with shared savings and overruns, which encourages cost control for both parties. Fixed-price leaves everything with the seller, and cost-plus or uncapped time and materials keeps the cost risk with the buyer.

S4Evaluation weights are technical 40%, price 40% and experience 20%. Bidder North scores 90, 60 and 80 on those criteria, and bidder South scores 70, 90 and 70 (higher is better). Which statement is correct?

  • ASouth ranks higher, with a weighted score of 78 against 76
  • BNorth ranks higher, because it has the strongest technical score
  • CThe bidders tie, because their simple averages are exactly equal
  • DNeither can be ranked until the price has been negotiated
Show the answer

Answer: A. The weighted score multiplies each score by its published weight: North gets 36 plus 24 plus 16, or 76, and South gets 28 plus 36 plus 14, or 78. Choosing on one criterion or on simple averages ignores the published weights.

S5A buyer needs 200 standard office chairs, and price is the main factor because several suppliers stock them. Which bid document fits best?

  • AA request for proposal, because vendors should propose their own solutions
  • BA request for quote, because price decides and the item is readily available
  • CA request for information, because the buyer wants to gather market data first
  • DA single-source agreement, because standard items need no competition
Show the answer

Answer: B. A request for quote suits readily available items where price is the main factor. A request for proposal is for complex scope where vendors propose solutions, a request for information gathers market data before bidding, and single sourcing skips competition.

S6During the bid period, one bidder emails the project manager a question that reveals an ambiguity in the statement of work. How should the project manager respond?

  • AAnswer privately and ask the bidder to keep the answer confidential
  • BAnswer the question for all bidders, giving each the same information
  • CIgnore the question, since clarifications might weaken the buyer's position
  • DAnswer only the bidder who asked, since it raised the question
Show the answer

Answer: B. The process must be transparent and fair, with questions answered adequately and to everyone so that all bidders hold the same information. Answering one bidder, ignoring the question or answering privately gives an unfair advantage or leaves the ambiguity.

S7After the bids arrive, a director asks to add a new evaluation criterion that happens to favor one bidder. What should the project manager do?

  • AAdd the criterion, since the director has authority over the evaluation
  • BCancel the tender and issue a new one that quietly includes the criterion
  • CAdd the criterion but give it a very small weight so the effect is limited
  • DKeep the published criteria and weights, and explain that changing them would be unfair
Show the answer

Answer: D. Selection follows the criteria and weights published in the tender documents, and they are not changed after bids arrive, because that undermines fairness and trust. Adding the criterion, even with a small weight, or quietly retendering to favor a bidder steers the award.

S8A vendor invites the project manager to sign the final contract at the end of a negotiation meeting, but the project manager has no authority to sign contracts. What should happen?

  • AThe procurement representative with signing authority concludes it, supported by the project manager
  • BThe project manager signs, since leading the project implies the authority
  • CThe project manager signs, then asks the sponsor to ratify the decision
  • DThe vendor signs alone and the buyer's signature is added later by the team
Show the answer

Answer: A. Negotiations are led by a procurement team member with authority to sign contracts, and the project manager supports with technical and project knowledge. Signing without authority, assuming it comes with the role or leaving the buyer's signature for later exposes the organization.

S9The project manager will support a negotiation for a major supply contract. What is the best first step?

  • AOpen with the lowest price demand to anchor the supplier's expectations
  • BClarify the project's priorities, limits and tradeable items, and the supplier's interests
  • CWait for the supplier's first offer and respond to each term as it appears
  • DLeave preparation to the supplier, who knows its own product best
Show the answer

Answer: B. A negotiation strategy starts from your priorities, limits and alternatives, plus an understanding of the other side's interests. Opening aggressively, waiting passively or leaving preparation to the supplier surrenders the information needed for a good agreement.

S10All proposals for a facility fit-out come in about 40% above the project manager's expectation, and the evaluation team asks what would help judge their reasonableness. What is the best answer?

  • AThe average of the proposals received, which reflects the market
  • BThe sponsor's budget figure, which defines what the work should cost
  • CThe bidder with the lowest proposal, which sets the reasonable price
  • DAn independent estimate prepared from market research and cost data
Show the answer

Answer: D. An independent estimate, built from market research and cost data, gives an objective yardstick for evaluating proposals. The lowest bid, the sponsor's budget or the average of the bids is only a reference point and may reflect the same bias or misjudgment.

S11A contractor on a hybrid program disputes payment for a variation order and threatens legal action. What is the best approach to the dispute?

  • AGo directly to litigation to show that the buyer will defend its position
  • BAgree to the contractor's claim to keep the relationship friendly
  • CNegotiate first, then use mediation or other ADR if needed, with careful records
  • DWithhold all payments to the contractor until the dispute is resolved
Show the answer

Answer: C. Disputes are escalated in steps: negotiation first, then alternative dispute resolution such as mediation or arbitration, with litigation as the last resort, while keeping factual records. Litigating at once, withholding all payments or conceding skips the proper path.

S12An owner wants the designer and the contractor involved from the start, sharing risks and rewards under one agreement, with open-book accounting. Which delivery approach is this?

  • AIntegrated project delivery, with a single multiparty agreement
  • BBuild-own-operate-transfer, in which the contractor operates the facility before handover
  • CTurnkey delivery, in which the contractor takes full responsibility for everything
  • DDesign-bid-build, with separate sequential contracts for design and construction
Show the answer

Answer: A. Integrated project delivery uses one multiparty agreement with early involvement, shared risks and rewards, collaborative decisions and open-book accounting. Design-bid-build separates the parties, turnkey places responsibility with one contractor, and BOOT adds operation before transfer.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1Why is procurement not a separate PMBOK 8 performance domain?

Show the answer

Project procurement usually runs through the organization's procurement department, policies and vendor relationships; PMBOK 8 covers sourcing strategy in Governance and procurement practices in Appendix X4.

R2What factors drive a make-or-buy decision?

Show the answer

Resource allocation, skills, need for specialized or independent expertise, avoiding permanent employment obligations, and the risks of each option; may use NPV, ROI, payback or cost-benefit analysis.

R3What does the sourcing strategy plan contain?

Show the answer

Insourcing or outsourcing decisions with their rationale, and source selection criteria.

R4What does the procurement management plan include?

Show the answer

Coordination with the schedule, timetable, metrics, roles and authority, constraints and assumptions, legal jurisdiction and currency, bidding approach, independent estimates, bonds or insurance, and prequalified sellers.

R5RFI versus RFP versus RFQ versus IFB?

Show the answer

RFI gathers information; RFP asks for proposed solutions for complex scope; RFQ is for readily available solutions where price decides; IFB (ITT) is a formal call for bids.

R6Name the source selection methods.

Show the answer

Least cost, qualifications only, quality-based (highest technical proposal score), quality and cost based, single source and fixed budget.

R7Give examples of source selection criteria.

Show the answer

Capability and capacity, product and life cycle cost, delivery dates, technical approach, relevant experience, key team qualifications, financial stability, compliance expertise, knowledge transfer and training, sustainability credentials.

R8Name the four fundamental contract types.

Show the answer

Fixed-price, cost-reimbursable, time and materials, and target-cost.

R9Who carries the cost risk under fixed-price and cost-reimbursable contracts?

Show the answer

Fixed-price: the seller. Cost-reimbursable: the buyer.

R10Name the emerging contracting practices.

Show the answer

Agile, smart, outcome-based, sustainable and collaborative contracting.

R11List the ADR methods.

Show the answer

Negotiation, mediation, arbitration, dispute review boards, expert determination, with litigation as the last resort.

R12What is a procurement audit?

Show the answer

A structured review of contracts and contracting processes for completeness, accuracy and effectiveness; rights and obligations are described in the contract.

R13Who leads contract negotiations?

Show the answer

A procurement team member with authority to sign contracts; the project manager and team assist.

R14What information may procurement phases include?

Show the answer

Sequencing and objectives of each phase, performance indicators and milestones, criteria for moving between phases, a monitoring and evaluation plan, and a knowledge transfer process.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Domain status Not a separate domain; Plan Sourcing Strategy (Governance) plus Appendix X4
Make or buy Expertise, headcount, risk, cost; outsource transfers delivery risk
Sourcing strategy plan Insource or outsource decisions and source selection criteria
Procurement plan Timetable, metrics, roles, constraints, jurisdiction, bidding, estimates, bonds, prequalified sellers
Bid documents RFI (information), RFP (solution), RFQ (price), IFB/ITT
Fair process Equal information, published weighted criteria, policy on gifts and conflicts
Selection methods Least cost, qualifications only, quality-based, quality and cost, single source, fixed budget
Contract types Fixed-price (seller risk), cost-reimbursable (buyer risk), T&M, target-cost
Choosing Defined scope → fixed; uncertain or risky → cost-reimbursable; evolving with a cap → T&M not-to-exceed; agile → incremental
Negotiation Led by the signing authority; know priorities, interests and alternatives; tie terms to goals
Administering Monitor metrics, inspect, formal change control, audit, joint recovery, record vendor performance
Disputes Negotiation → mediation → other ADR → arbitration → litigation; keep records
Closing Resolve disputes and payments; close all contracts before the project
Emerging Agile, collaborative, outcome-based, sustainable (ESG), smart contracts; AI analysis
Delivery solution Build, buy, lease, adapt, partner; buy-and-close-gap beats a long custom build Beyond PMBOK 8
First-action pattern Check the plan and contract, act under its terms, change through change control, escalate in steps, keep records, record performance
